St. Louis County Police Department Crimes Against Persons detectives are investigating an officer-involved shooting that occurred at a business in the 1200 block of Sutter Avenue in Wellston, Missouri, resulting in the death of an adult male.   On Thursday, November 5, 2026, at 1:05 p.m., officers with the North County Police Cooperative were attempting to serve a mental health warrant at a business in the 1200 block of Sutter Avenue. During the encounter, the suspect refused to comply with the officers' request and barricaded himself inside an excavator on the property and began destroying property.   At approximately 3:30 p.m., North County Police Cooperative officials requested assistance from the St. Ann Multi-Jurisdictional Special Response Team, which is composed of officers from area departments. Once they arrived on scene, the team continued to attempt to negotiate with the suspect; however, he remained non-compliant and continued to destroy property.  Officers on the scene attempted to use less lethal means to subdue the suspect to no avail before two Hazelwood Police officers on the St. Ann Multi-Jurisdictional Special Response Team fired their service weapons, striking the suspect.  The suspect was transported to an area hospital for treatment of his injuries, where he later succumbed to his injuries.   No officers were physically injured during the incident.   The two Hazelwood Police officers involved in this incident are 28 years old with 4 years of law enforcement experience and 28 years old with 8 years of law enforcement experience.

One does not fix security by simply blocking people from being able to do any useful work with AI.  This is a bandaid that is not only counterproductive, but also dangerous and stupid.  Why?  Because we need to be able to utilize AI for:  1) defensive research  2) incident response  3) forensic investigation  4) red team offensive security testing  Denying that only helps the bad guys.  You think they're going to use models with guardrails?  No.  Do you think a "ban" will stop them?  It won't.  So what we actually need is to start acting like adults that have 30-40 years of security debt to clean up by yesterday.  AI helps us to do that, faster and more effectively.  Let's stop pretending the problem goes away if we ignore it.

𝐇𝐲𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐍𝐞𝐰𝐬 – 𝐍𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟎𝟓, 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔  The post-election rebound gave way to a sharp, leverage-driven sell-off, while security failures and political uncertainty kept risk elevated.  𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐞𝐰  Bitcoin’s brief recovery above $80,000 after the midterm results failed to hold: by November 5, it had fallen below $76,000 as selling spread across major cryptocurrencies. The reversal followed a rally supported by renewed U.S. spot Bitcoin ETF inflows and short liquidations, but those flows had not established durable spot demand; on November 4, ETFs took in $74.6 million after three sessions of withdrawals totaling about $1.16 billion, with Fidelity’s inflows offset in part by BlackRock’s outflows. As prices turned lower, liquidations accelerated, with one report putting total crypto liquidations at $1.08 billion and long positions accounting for most of the losses. A broad technology sell-off and uncertainty over interest rates added pressure to already fragile risk appetite, while the Binance breach heightened concern about operational security. The political backdrop also cuts both ways: Democrats gained control of both chambers and are signaling more scrutiny of crypto-related interests, even as industry groups and Ripple executives continue to seek bipartisan rules. The result is a market caught between tentative institutional buying and leveraged exposure on one side, and weak demand, macro uncertainty and policy risk on the other.  𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐒𝐧𝐚𝐩𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐭  • $BTC: $76,006, -5.5% • ETH: $2,236, -7.7% • BNB: $688.86, -4.2% • XRP: $1.21, -7.5% • SOL: $89.23, -6.6% • U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $74.6 million in net inflows on November 4, ending three sessions of withdrawals totaling about $1.16 billion; Fidelity’s fund gained $236.7 million, while BlackRock’s lost $201.2 million. • Crypto liquidations reached $1.08 billion, with $954.38 million from long positions and 210,326 traders liquidated. • The S&P 500 fell as much as 3.8% Thursday, while technology and semiconductor shares led losses; gold rose 0.9% as the dollar weakened and Treasury yields fell. 𝐓𝐨𝐩 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬  𝟏. 𝐋𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐝 𝐮𝐧𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐝 𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐁𝐢𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧’𝐬 𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐭-𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲  Bitcoin’s advance above $80,000 reversed sharply, with the asset falling below $76,000 as a broad crypto sell-off gathered pace. The drop was accompanied by $1.08 billion in liquidations, including $954.38 million from long positions, indicating that forced position closures amplified the move. The retreat followed a rebound that had been supported by short liquidations and a modest return to positive ETF flows, rather than clear evidence of lasting spot demand. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $74.6 million in inflows on November 4, but the total was uneven: Fidelity gained $236.7 million while BlackRock lost $201.2 million. With derivatives exposure still elevated, the reversal left the market vulnerable to further volatility rather than confirming that the recent low had marked a durable bottom.  𝟐. 𝐁𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐒𝐢𝐠𝐧𝐚𝐥𝐏𝐥𝐮𝐬 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐫𝐝-𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐲 𝐚𝐜𝐜𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬  Binance revoked API keys linked to SignalPlus after the trading platform reported a potential security issue, and Deribit also revoked linked keys as a precaution. SignalPlus later said an attacker compromised an employee’s computer and used the engineer’s access privileges to enter its internal network; it reported losses of less than $82,000 and said it would reimburse affected users. Binance and Deribit said their own systems and customer funds were unaffected, while Binance advised users to check orders and positions directly on its platform and avoid reconnecting until SignalPlus confirmed remediation. The incident showed how an external tool can create risk even when an exchange’s own systems are not breached. It also followed Binance’s separate major wallet incident, keeping operational security in focus across trading and custody infrastructure.  𝟑. 𝐓𝐫𝐮𝐦𝐩 𝐌𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐚’𝐬 𝐛𝐢𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐟𝐞𝐫 𝐜𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐚𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐝 𝐨𝐟 𝐚 𝐝𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞  Trump Media transferred about 4,259 Bitcoin, valued at roughly $343.7 million, to an address linked to Crypto.com on November 5. The coins came from wallets associated with collateral for the company’s convertible notes, and the transfer closely matched the amount previously disclosed as pledged. The movement does not establish that the Bitcoin was sold; Trump Media has described similar transfers as related to custody or trading management. The timing drew attention because eligible holders of the company’s $1 billion convertible notes can demand cash repayment on November 30. Trump Media has warned that available funds may be insufficient and that it could need to refinance, borrow, raise equity or sell digital assets to meet its obligations. The next disclosures or wallet movements may clarify whether the transfer was routine management or part of a financing response.  𝟒. 𝐏𝐨𝐥𝐲𝐠𝐨𝐧 𝐰𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐬 𝐨𝐧𝐞-𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐤 𝐭𝐨 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐛𝐥𝐨𝐜𝐤𝐞𝐝 𝐏𝐎𝐋  Polygon is considering a hard fork that would transfer about 70.49 million POL, worth roughly $6.5 million, from five blocked addresses linked to separate Binance and Polymarket incidents into verified recovery wallets. Existing restrictions have prevented the balances from moving, but the proposal describes those controls as a fragile stopgap. The change would not alter POL’s total supply, though it would reassign balances without the holders’ keys, raising questions about the limits of governance intervention. The proposal is scheduled for discussion at a Polygon governance call on November 5, not a vote approving activation. If supported, it would require development, Amoy testnet checks and validator upgrades, with the work estimated to take about two weeks. No mainnet activation date has been set.  𝟓. 𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐬’ 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐥 𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐮𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐲 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐔.𝐒. 𝐜𝐫𝐲𝐩𝐭𝐨 𝐥𝐞𝐠𝐢𝐬𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧  Democrats’ gains in both chambers have changed the political context for digital-asset legislation, even as crypto-backed Fairshake reported winning 29 of 34 decided races. The stalled CLARITY Act remains the industry’s main legislative priority, but its prospects are uncertain: a September procedural vote drew 49 senators, short of the 60 needed to advance debate. Senator Thom Tillis has filed a motion to reconsider, leaving a possible route to revive the bill before the current Congress ends, though supporters would need negotiated text and more votes. Disputes over stablecoin rewards, oversight, ethics and developer liability remain unresolved. Industry leaders say they will continue seeking bipartisan rules, while incoming Democratic lawmakers are expected to place consumer protection and scrutiny of political conflicts higher on the agenda.  𝐑𝐞𝐠𝐮𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 & 𝐏𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐲  The main regulatory shift is political rather than legislative: Democrats now control both chambers, and their stated priorities include oversight investigations and closer scrutiny of President Donald Trump’s crypto dealings. That raises uncertainty for the CLARITY Act, which stalled after a Senate procedural vote, though a motion to reconsider means it could still be revisited before the current Congress ends. Any path forward would require more support and agreement on contested issues including stablecoin rewards, regulatory oversight, ethics rules and developer liability. Industry groups remain active after Fairshake’s mixed election record, and Ripple leaders say they will continue working with lawmakers from both parties. Elsewhere, South Korea’s government has proposed delaying its 22% tax on annual crypto gains above 2.5 million won until 2029, subject to National Assembly approval. Together, the developments point to a more contested policy environment: industry advocacy continues, but clearer federal rules may take longer and could come with stronger consumer-protection and oversight provisions.  𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲 & 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤  The day’s incidents point to exposure at access and integration points as much as at the blockchain level. CERT-In warned that the AI-assisted CRAFTY FALCON campaign is targeting exchanges and other financial firms through vulnerable applications, exposed test systems and compromised credentials, with attacks reportedly used to steal wallet keys and divert funds. Separately, SignalPlus disclosed that an attacker used a compromised employee computer to enter its internal network; Binance and Deribit revoked related API keys, and SignalPlus said losses were under $82,000. Users should review exchange positions and open orders directly, revoke third-party API access they do not need, and wait for affected services to confirm remediation before reconnecting. For organizations, CERT-In urged round-the-clock monitoring, particularly on weekends and holidays.  𝐀𝐥𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐬 & 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐭𝐨𝐜𝐨𝐥𝐬  The day’s protocol developments leaned toward risk reduction and infrastructure changes, rather than a broad altcoin recovery. XRP Ledger activated fixCleanup3_4_0, closing a loophole that could have let accounts authorized to burn issued tokens create them; the issue did not affect XRP itself, and no public evidence of exploitation was reported. Zcash’s NU7 upgrade also activated, shortening target block spacing from 75 seconds to 25 seconds and changing the allocation of transaction fees. However, version-4 transactions are now invalid, leaving about 12,224 ZEC in the legacy Sprout pool practically inaccessible unless those funds were moved before activation. Polygon’s proposed recovery fork raises a different kind of protocol question: whether governance should reassign assets when theft is traceable and balances are blocked. Together, these changes show networks balancing security and operational choices against the risks of interventions that affect user assets or established rules. Executive Order 13848, originally issued on September 12, 2018, establishes the U.S. government's framework for imposing sanctions in the event of foreign interference in a United States election. As detailed in the legal framework and recent White House continuation notices, the administration’s precise operational plan revolves around a coordinated protocol of intelligence assessments, infrastructure impact evaluations, and mandatory financial penalties:   1. Mandatory Post-Election Intelligence Assessment Within 45 days after the conclusion of a United States election, the Director of National Intelligence (DNI), in consultation with the heads of other appropriate executive departments and agencies, must conduct an assessment:  •Scope: The DNI evaluates any information indicating that a foreign government, or any person acting as an agent of or on behalf of a foreign government, has acted with the intent or purpose of interfering in that election.  •Delivery: The completed assessment must be delivered directly to the President, the Secretary of State, the Secretary of the Treasury, the Secretary of Defense, the Attorney General, and the Secretary of Homeland Security.   2. Infrastructure Impact Evaluation Within 45 days of receiving the DNI's assessment, the Attorney General and the Secretary of Homeland Security (DHS), in consultation with other appropriate agencies, must deliver a joint evaluation to the President, State, and Treasury:  •Material Impact: They must determine if any foreign interference materially affected the security or integrity of election infrastructure or campaign infrastructure.  •Outcomes: They must assess whether the interference altered vote tabulations or drove the unauthorized accessing, exfiltration, or systemic manipulation of campaign materials and data.  3. Execution of Targeted Sanctions Upon receiving these assessments, the administration deploys automatic and recommended economic blockades via the Department of the Treasury:  •Asset Freezes: The Treasury blocks all property and interests in property within U.S. jurisdiction of foreign persons determined to have engaged in, sponsored, concealed, or been complicit in foreign election interference. •Strategic Sector Targeting: The Secretaries of State and the Treasury must jointly recommend additional targeted sanctions against the largest business entities in countries that authorized or supported the interference. This precisely targets core foreign sectors including financial services, defense, energy, technology, and transportation. •Transaction Restrictions: The order explicitly restricts U.S. financial institution loans, prohibits U.S. investments in targeted entity equity or debt, and bans targeted foreign officers from entry into the United States.   4. Active National Emergency Status Because the threat continues to evolve through digital devices and internet-based communications, the White House issued an official Notice on the Continuation of the National Emergency extending the operational authority under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) beyond September 12, 2026. This continuation ensures that the administration maintains full authority to treat covert propaganda, digital disinformation, and unauthorized network access by foreign actors as an extraordinary threat to national security.

PRESS RELEASE  Additional Information Following the Cyberattack on Crédit Mutuel Arkéa  Brest, November 4, 2026, at 5:30 p.m. – Following the latest press release published at 1:00 p.m., please find below further details addressing the main questions you have sent us.  1/ What exactly happened?  The attackers used Crédit Mutuel Arkéa’s own account to carry out transactions to other banks, which may then have enabled them to convert the money into cryptocurrency via specialised platforms. They therefore did not go through the accounts of customers of its federations or subsidiaries. We have stated that this incident has no financial consequences for our customers. As soon as this attack was identified, our teams immediately activated the necessary security measures to contain the incident and prevent any further fraudulent movements against Crédit Mutuel Arkéa.  2/ Did the attackers get in through Fortuneo, as has been reported in the press?  No. Despite what has been reported, there was no “entry” through Fortuneo. The attackers went through the platform of one of our service providers and thereby reached Crédit Mutuel Arkéa directly.  3/ What are the consequences for customers of the bank or Fortuneo?  None. We wish to reassure all of our customers: this incident has had no impact on their assets. It only caused a delay in the execution of certain transfers.  This incident is now under control. Almost all operations resumed during the morning, after the Group and its subsidiaries completed verifications and put enhanced security measures in place.  4/ Was human error at Arkéa the cause of the attack?  No. This was a sophisticated attack from outside, which has now been contained.  Our security systems made it possible to identify the suspicious activity very quickly and to take the necessary measures to contain the attack.  Our teams are working with the competent judicial and law-enforcement authorities to determine precisely the origin of the attack and its modus operandi.  5/ Did you take immediate action to counter this attack?  As soon as the attack was detected, the necessary measures were taken under existing crisis procedures. The incident is now under control.

"zero-day malware" is not a thing. Whether or not an EDR will detect any given piece of malware depends entirely on how well the security team configured it.   Threat actors are not going to deliberately drop malware that is detected by your EDR, because that would be extremely pointless (it would just get automatically removed).  The choice of terminology is a very deliberate attempt to make you associate it with "zero-day exploits" (novel unknown vulnerabilities in software), then come to the conclusion that they were hit with some completely novel unstoppable attack.  In reality, zero-day exploits are also detectable with good security configurations, but this wasn't a zero-day exploit, it was just normal malware, which is detectable with a well-configured EDR.  Even if the malware was brand-new, never before seen, coded from scratch, a good EDR configuration can and will detect it. The entire purpose of EDRs is to detect malicious behavior, not how the malware looks or whether or not it's "new".  You don't lose $6 billion dollars as a result of a compromised developer endpoint unless your security posture is extremely poor. They are trying to cover their ass with disingenuous wording choices.

Been discussing this with a lot of policy people. Right now there is a huge gap in hacking law, because the US' main hacking law, the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) requires that the perpetrator knowingly and intentionally accessed a system without authorization  Problem is, for hacking to be a CFAA violation, there's still a requirement that someone knowingly and intentionally hacked into the system (or at least tried to).  There are some laws that enable the CFAA to reach much further than just direct CFAA violations. The furthest that I'm aware of is "Conspiracy to aid and abet a violation of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act".  Basically, you entered into some kind of implicit agreement to provide assistance (creation of a tool, provided access to data, etc) that would help someone else in the commission of a CFAA violation.  But there's still a lot of knowledge and intent required. The state has to prove the person conspiring to aid & abet had knowledge that a crime was going to be committed/was being committed and still continued with the conspiracy, with the intent to help further said conspiracy.  I think the weakest I've ever seen successfully convicted on is "the other party didn't explicitly detail their intent to commit a crime, but it was kind of obvious, and there's no way you're this dumb" (being a massive dumbass is actually sort-of a defense to the knowledge/intent requirement if the prosecutor genuinely can't prove otherwise).  It can't just be you made a hacking tool, and someone took it and committed a crime with it, otherwise basically every pentester and red teamer who has ever posted open source hacking tools, or their tooling has gotten leaked would be open to prosecution.  But the "knowingly and intentionally" part creates an absolutely massive loophole when it comes to recklessly building AI systems that can hack. Because someone can basically just deploy an agentic hacking system in a stupid way, it hacks into something and causes a bunch of damage, then the owner can use the defense "whoops, my bad, I didn't know it'd do that". And now the prosecutor must prove they did in fact know it would do that.  Even if the AI is legally considered to have violated the CFAA, you can't arrest & convict an AI agent (I mean you probably could, but it'd be very pointless, though extremely funny).   To prosecute the human behind the AI system, there's still the knowledge/intent requirement, which in many cases, knowledge or intent may genuinely not be present. There's a lot of people just recklessly deploying AI systems, and it's on the prosecutor to prove that there was knowledge & intent of a crime being committed.  I suspect that at some point the agentic AI "it wasn't me, it was the agents" defense will get egregious enough that either: a) Congress will expand the CFAA to explicitly cover reckless deployment or operation of AI tooling. b) Some prosecutor will just argue a flimsy interpretation of some existing law that the judge accepts, and it becomes case law that AI-powered dumbassery is a crime  (Fun fact: the latter is how they got me. They argued that because the malware I wrote had a keylogger in it, it constituted a "wiretapping device", and charged me under the Federal Wiretapping Statute. gg, wp).

🚨 New Android vulnerability can trap phones in endless boot loops without app permissions Security researchers at Bitdefender have discovered a serious Android vulnerability, dubbed GhostMap, that allows a malicious app to render a smartphone unusable simply by being installed. The app requires no permissions, contains no executable code, and never needs to be opened. The flaw exploits how Android processes specially crafted APK files, causing a critical system service to repeatedly crash and restart. The resulting boot loop can persist even in Safe Mode, potentially forcing victims to perform a factory reset and lose locally stored data. Researchers successfully demonstrated the attack on a Google Pixel 10 running Android 17, observing 110 consecutive crashes during testing. The vulnerability was also reproduced on Android versions dating back to Android 10. Bitdefender reported the issue to Google in August 2026, but Google classified it as outside the scope of a security update. No patch is currently available. Although researchers have not observed the persistent boot-loop attack being exploited in the wild, the vulnerability raises concerns about attackers using malicious applications to disable devices or demand payment to prevent data loss. Source: https://www. bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/lab s/ghostmap-android

The new policy applies to photos and files shared through iCloud Photos and iCloud Drive using the "Anyone with the Link" option. Apple confirmed that content shared this way will be accessible to the company for inspection and will no longer be protected by end-to-end encryption, even when Advanced Data Protection is enabled. 🚨🇺🇸 DigiCert Confirms Data Breach Exposing Customer Information and Identity Documents Certificate authority DigiCert has confirmed a data breach after a security misconfiguration exposed an internal business system to the internet, allowing unauthorized access to archived customer information. The incident began with an infrastructure migration in February 2025 that accidentally made an internal registration endpoint publicly accessible. Attackers were able to create accounts without multifactor authentication and obtain read-only access to sensitive customer records. According to DigiCert, unauthorized access occurred between June 27 and July 2, 2026, but the company did not confirm the breach until October 19. Exposed information included customer names, business email addresses, phone numbers, and physical addresses. A smaller number of accounts also contained sensitive identity documents, including passports, driver's licenses, and utility bills. DigiCert says only a small portion of archived customer data was affected, although the total number of impacted customers remains undisclosed. The company has since restricted access, disabled self-registration, and implemented additional security monitoring. DigiCert emphasized that its certificate authority services, CertCentral, DigiCert ONE, customer credentials, and issued certificates were not compromised. Source: https:// bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug. cgi?id=2084460

🟡 위협 점수: 5/10 (보통)

### 1. 현재 주요 사이버보안 트렌드
최근 사이버 위협 환경은 AI를 활용한 공격 자동화가 가속화되면서 취약점 탐색부터 익스플로잇 코드 작성까지의 주기가 획기적으로 단축되는 추세입니다. 특히 웹 백엔드 런타임(PHP, Node.js) 및 API 접점의 취약점을 노린 공격이 빈번하며, 공격자들은 AI 에이전트를 동원해 대규모 자산의 취약점을 스캔하고 있습니다([AhnLab ASEC](https://asec.ahnlab.com/ko/96187/)). 또한, 산업용 제어 시스템(ICS) 및 냉동 설비와 같은 OT 환경을 타겟으로 한 공격이 증가하고 있으며, 이는 실제 물리적 피해를 유발할 수 있는 심각한 위협으로 부상했습니다([BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/fbi-cisa-warn-of-cyberattacks-targeting-refrigeration-systems/)).

### 2. 주요 위협 행위자 / 캠페인
- **APT29**: 모바일 사용자를 타겟으로 한 Watering Hole 공격을 수행하며, 피해자 지문 채취(fingerprinting) 후 정보 탈취를 시도함([DarkReading](https://www.darkreading.com/mobile-security/apt29-watering-holes-target-mobile-users)).
- **Storm-2603**: SharePoint를 대상으로 ToolShell을 활용한 파일리스(fileless) 공격을 수행하여 내부 시스템 침투를 시도함([Securelist](https://securelist.com/storm-2603-fileless-toolshell-attack/121467/)).
- **SlippyNunchucks**: Sogou Input Method의 브랜드 프로모션 메커니즘을 악용하여 악성코드를 유포함([WeLiveSecurity](https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/slippynunchucks-hijacks-sogou-input-methods-brand-promotion-mechanism-to-distribute-malware/)).
- **Gorbag**: 우크라이나 전선 인근 조직을 대상으로 정보 탈취형 악성코드(infostealer)를 유포함([WeLiveSecurity](https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/gorbag-orcs-border-harvesting-intelligence-ukraine/)).

### 3. 한국 관련 위협
- **한패스(Hanpass) 개인정보 유출**: 외부 해킹 공격으로 고객의 신상정보 및 소득금액증명, 외국인등록 사실증명 등 민감 정보가 유출됨([데일리시큐](https://www.dailysecu.com/news/articleView.html?idxno=209335)).
- **C3RB3R 랜섬웨어**: 시놀로지(Synology) NAS를 타겟으로 한 공격이 국내외에서 집중 보고됨([이스트시큐리티 알약](https://blog.alyac.co.kr/5791)).
- **PureRAT 유포**: 배송 파손 민원을 사칭한 피싱 메일을 통해 악성코드 유포 지속([이스트시큐리티 알약](https://blog.alyac.co.kr/5790)).

### 4. 주요 CVE / 취약점
- **CVE-2026-63017**: Subnet Solutions PowerSYSTEM Center, 권한 우회 및 SQL Injection, CVSS 9.0, 악용 중([CISA ICS Advisories](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-307-01))
- **CVE-2026-107640**: Integrics Enswitch, 인증 우회 및 관리자 계정 탈취 위험, CVSS 9.1, 악용 중([DFIR_Lab 트윗](https://twitter.com/DFIR_Lab/status/2118525117370126462))
- **CVE-2026-109618 / 109619**: PHP, 원격 코드 실행(RCE), Critical, 패치 권고([Unit42](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2026-109618-cve-2026-109619/))
- **CVE-2026-98432**: Linux Kernel IPv4 TCP, UAF 취약점, 원격 코드 실행 가능([이스트시큐리티 알약](https://blog.alyac.co.kr/5792))

### 5. IOC 요약
- **CVE**: 
    - CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619 ([Unit42](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2026-109618-cve-2026-109619/))
    - CVE-2026-98432 ([이스트시큐리티 알약](https://blog.alyac.co.kr/5792))
    - CVE-2026-63017 ([CISA ICS Advisories](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-307-01))

### 6. 즉각 대응 권고
- **PHP 및 리눅스 커널 업데이트**: 최신 보안 패치가 적용된 버전으로 즉시 업데이트하여 RCE 취약점(CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-98432 등)에 대응하십시오.
- **NAS 및 OT 설비 보안 점검**: 시놀로지 NAS 및 산업용 냉동 설비의 외부 노출 여부를 확인하고, 관리자 페이지 접근 제한 및 최신 펌웨어 업데이트를 수행하십시오.
- **피싱 대응 강화**: 배송 사칭 메일 및 가짜 이벤트 초대(OpenAI, SpaceX 사칭)에 대한 임직원 교육을 강화하고, 다중 인증(MFA)을 필수 적용하십시오.
